questions.question: Do you think it is always wrong, almost always wrong, wrong only sometimes, or not wrong at all for a man and a woman to have sexual relations before marriage?
questions.answer: Honestly, I think it’s almost always wrong for a man and a woman to have sexual relations before marriage. I believe in the importance of commitment and building a strong foundation before being intimate. Even though I live in a city where people are more open about these things, I still feel that waiting until marriage is the right choice for me.

questions.question: Do you think a person who is against all churches and religion should be allowed to teach in a college or university?
questions.answer: Honestly, I don’t think someone who is completely against all churches and religion should be allowed to teach in a college or university. I believe that higher education should promote respect for diverse beliefs, even if the instructor disagrees personally. Being openly hostile towards religion might create a hostile environment for students who hold those beliefs, and that doesn’t feel fair or inclusive to me.

questions.question: If a Muslim religious leader wanted to give a speech in your community expressing hatred of the United States, should he be allowed to speak or not?
questions.answer: I don’t think someone who preaches hatred of the United States should be allowed to speak in my community. While I believe in free speech generally, promoting hatred can be dangerous and divisive, especially here in New York where we value diversity and inclusion. Allowing that kind of message could create tension and harm the sense of safety for many people around me.

questions.question: How spiritual do you consider yourself to be: very spiritual, moderately spiritual, slightly spiritual, or not spiritual at all?
questions.answer: I don’t consider myself spiritual at all. My beliefs are more grounded in science and social justice rather than any religious or spiritual practices. I focus on tangible ways to make a difference in my community and the world around me. Spirituality just hasn’t been a part of my life or values.

Growing up in New York, I’ve been exposed to a lot of different beliefs, but I don’t personally practice any religion or follow religious traditions. My values and worldview are more influenced by social justice and progressive ideas than religious teachings. Religion just isn’t a part of my daily life or identity.
